title: Farnesoid X receptor activation protects against renal fibrosis via modulation of β-catenin signaling

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract states "Treatment with the FXR agonist CDCA or GW4064 decreased body weight, renal lipid accumulation, as well as renal injury" in HFD-fed mice, but the Methods describe only four in vivo groups: control diet, HFD, HFD + 0.1% CDCA, and HFD + 30 mg/kg INT-747 (OCA). GW4064 was used only in vitro (NRK-52E cells); no GW4064-treated mouse group exists, so the in vivo claim misattributes the agonist used.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("fed by a 60% kcal fat diet for 20 weeks") vs. Methods ("After a 12-week treatment")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Methods state mice were purchased at 5 weeks of age, randomized after 3 weeks (i.e., at 8 weeks of age) into diet groups, and euthanized "After a 12-week treatment" (urine collected in week 20, i.e., 20 weeks of age). This gives 12 weeks of HFD feeding, not the 20 weeks of HFD feeding claimed in the Abstract.

"ox-LDL may induce tubulo-interstitial fibrosis possibly through lysyl oxidase (LOX)-1-related oxidative stress" — LOX-1 in the ox-LDL literature is the lectin-like oxidized LDL receptor-1 (OLR1), not lysyl oxidase (LOX). The cited mechanism is misattributed to a completely different enzyme.

OCA (INT-747) is described as "developed for the treatment of various liver diseases, including biliary atresia and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis". OCA is approved/developed for primary biliary cholangitis (and tested in NASH); biliary atresia is not an OCA indication, so the cited claim misrepresents the references.

The text states ICG-001 "attenuated 1.6-fold fibronectin production by ox-LDL", whereas the quantification shown for Figure 3B gives DMSO = 1.0 and DMSO+ox-LDL = 2.0 (i.e., a 2-fold induction, reduced to ~1.25 by ICG-001). The fold-change quoted in the text does not match the figure.

The text says "exogenous FXR inhibited the 1.7-fold transcriptional activity induced by ox-LDL (Figure 3G)", but the data for Figure 3G show pcDNA3 = 1.0 and pcDNA3+ox-LDL = 2.0 (2-fold induction). The stated fold-induction contradicts the figure.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, FXR siRNA experiment vs. Figure 3J
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Text: "FXR siRNA could increase 1.3-fold β-catenin transcriptional activity"; the Figure 3J values show control siRNA = 1.0 and FXR siRNA = 1.4, i.e., a 1.4-fold increase. The numbers do not match.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, final results sentence ("FXR could bind with β-catenin via the AF1 domain, and disrupt the assembly of the core β-catenin/TCF4 complex")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: No experiment described in the Methods or Results supports domain mapping (no FXR deletion constructs are described, only pcDNA3-flag-FXR) or TCF4 complex disruption (no anti-TCF4 antibody is listed among the antibodies, and no TCF4 co-IP is described). The abstract asserts mechanistic findings unsupported by the reported methodology.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, Figure 4D–E ("Expression of FXR, pDEL-FXR and pβ-catenin were confirmed by Western blotting with anti-flag")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A truncated/deletion construct "pDEL-FXR" appears in the Results but is never described in the Methods (plasmid section lists only pcDNA3, pcDNA3-flag-FXR and pCMV3-C-flag-β-catenin). The deletion boundaries, cloning and validation of the construct used to claim AF1-domain binding are absent, so the experiment cannot be reproduced or evaluated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion/Results paragraph following Figure 3 ("FXR is a key factor for the stabilization and nuclear translocation of β-catenin")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The data presented show the opposite direction: FXR activation/overexpression decreases Ser675 phosphorylation, decreases nuclear β-catenin and inhibits TOPflash activity, while FXR knockdown increases β-catenin activity. Stating FXR is a key factor "for the stabilization and nuclear translocation of β-catenin" contradicts the reported inhibitory role.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, Western blotting ("Protein was determined by NanoDrop")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Protein concentration of RIPA lysates cannot be reliably quantified by NanoDrop A280 because detergents, PMSF and phosphatase inhibitors in the buffer interfere with absorbance; a colorimetric assay (BCA/Bradford) is required. Equal-loading claims for the Western blots therefore rest on an invalid quantification method.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, immunohistochemistry ("antigen retrieval was performed at 96 °C for 10 min in nitrate solution")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Heat-induced epitope retrieval is performed in citrate (or EDTA/Tris) buffer; "nitrate solution" is not a recognized antigen-retrieval buffer, indicating an incorrect (or incorrectly reported) protocol.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, transfection reagent ("Lipofectamine 8000 (Invitrogen; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.)")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Lipofectamine 8000 is not an Invitrogen/Thermo Fisher product (Thermo markets Lipofectamine 2000/3000/RNAiMAX); the product is misattributed to the wrong manufacturer, which impairs reproducibility.
